analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans personally import cheaper prescription drugs and lets pharmacists import them under FDA safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to let Americans import lower-priced prescription drugs never got a hearing or a vote, dying in a House subcommittee at the end of the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal drug law so that individual Americans could import prescription drugs that appear FDA-approved, non-narcotic, and made by a registered manufacturer, and it would require the government to set up a program letting licensed pharmacists import such drugs as well. The point is price: the same medicines often cost far less abroad, and importation lets Americans buy them at foreign prices. It excludes controlled substances and biological products, and allows alternative labeling to satisfy trademark rules. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay for prescription drugs out of pocket, especially seniors and the uninsured without negotiated drug coverage, who could buy FDA-approved medicines at foreign prices. Licensed pharmacies that import drugs would gain a new legal channel.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from preventing individuals not in the drug-import business from importing prescription drugs that appear to be FDA-approved, non-narcotic, and produced by a registered establishment [S3].

It requires HHS, within 180 days of enactment, to issue final rules and begin operating a program authorizing 'covered pharmacists' — pharmacists who otherwise lack import authority — to import such prescription drugs, subject to safety standards for adulterated, misbranded, or unapproved drugs [S3].

It excludes controlled substances in Schedules I through III and biological products from importation, and allows alternative labeling so imported drugs are not deemed misbranded while complying with trademark law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose United States sales depend on keeping American prices above the lower prices charged abroad, and to a lesser extent wholesalers and distributors whose controlled domestic supply chain would face new foreign competition.

drawbacks.text: Personal importation bypasses the closed U.S. drug distribution chain, and the FDA has long argued it cannot verify the safety of medicines shipped from foreign pharmacies, creating risk of counterfeit or mishandled products even with the bill's screening standards [S3].

The bill relies on appearance-based screening — drugs must only 'appear' approved and made by a registered establishment — and gives the Secretary discretion over pharmacist-importation procedures, which critics could call too loose to guarantee authenticity [S3].
Allowing alternative labeling for imported drugs weakens standard U.S. packaging and labeling requirements for those products in order to accommodate foreign trademarks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is real and large: identical FDA-approved medicines often sell for a fraction of the U.S. price in Canada and Europe, and importation is one of the few direct ways to arbitrage that gap. The safety objection is genuine but manageable — the bill's standards (FDA-approved appearance, registered manufacturer, no controlled substances or biologics) plus a regulated pharmacist program are a more guarded design than free-form personal importation. The main reason the bill failed was not its drafting but the industry's stake in preserving the price difference.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the 107th Congress, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2003 [S5],[S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2002 by Rep. Jack Kingston with 20 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans such as Gutknecht, Thune, and Shays and Democrats such as Crowley, Baldacci, and Pomeroy [S3],[S4].

It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on July 29, 2002 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill reached only the introductory stage: no committee report, no markup, and no vote appears anywhere in its action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept the status quo: Americans continued paying U.S. prices rather than foreign prices for their medicines, and no competing importation channel was opened. Consumers who would have used the program gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jack Kingston
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Drug Importation Act of 2002 and recruited 20 original cosponsors from both parties [S3],[S4].

for.name: 17 of 223 House Republicans and 4 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Republicans Gutknecht, Thune, Stump, Kolbe, Shays, Tancredo, and Hoekstra and Democrats Crowley, Baldacci, and Pomeroy [S4].

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chairman, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never brought the bill before the full committee or scheduled it for consideration; it stayed in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed importation legislation on safety and supply-chain grounds, arguing foreign-sourced drugs could not be verified; importation proposals threatened billions in U.S. sales priced above foreign prices.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but leaned Republican: of the bill's 21 cosponsors, 17 were Republicans and 4 were Democrats [S4], and no party bloc ever got the chance to vote on it.

industries.note: Importation would let Americans buy the same FDA-approved medicines at the lower prices charged abroad, directly cutting into the higher U.S. prices that are the industry's main profit pool. The industry fought importation legislation throughout this era on safety grounds. Sources record the bill's price-opening mechanism [S3]; the industry's opposition is well-documented public reporting.

The bill creates a regulated legal channel for licensed pharmacists to import prescription drugs, giving pharmacies a new supply option and letting them pass foreign prices to customers. Stance is aligned: pharmacies gain by serving customers cheaper drugs. [S3]

The closed domestic distribution chain would face new competition from a parallel import channel authorized for pharmacists, though registered firms could participate in approved chains of distribution. [S3]
